parent.name: Question lifecycle
parent.one_liner: A reference code and four statuses carry each question to its answer
parent.explain: I give every landlord question a short reference code and a status, and the status shows where it stands. A question starts as auto_answered when a saved answer matched, or not_sent when none did. It becomes waiting once the renter says yes and I send it, then replied when the landlord answers. The landlord's reply can also be saved as a new answer, so the next renter asking the same thing gets it instantly.
parent.why: Each MCP call, one request from the model, arrives on its own, so the code and status are the only memory of a question. Without four clear statuses, I could not stop a double send or know when a reply is due.

children.name: Reference code
children.one_liner: Each question gets a short readable code the model passes back
children.explain: I mint a reference code as Q plus five random characters, drawn with Python's secrets module, which is meant for hard-to-predict picks. The five characters come from 31 symbols with no 0, O, 1, I or L, so a code reads aloud cleanly. Each MCP call arrives alone, so I return the code and the model passes it back as a plain argument. The code's status is one of four words: auto_answered, not_sent, waiting or replied.
children.why: Nothing remembers an earlier call, so a later call needs a handle to name the question it means. Look-alike characters such as 0 and O would be misread when a code is spoken or typed. Redrawing a taken code keeps two questions from sharing one.

children.name: Consent gate
children.one_liner: A question reaches the landlord only after the renter says yes
children.explain: I want a question to reach the landlord only after the renter says yes, and two things carry that rule. First, my server instructions tell the model to call send_question_to_landlord only after a clear yes, and the tool's own description repeats it. Second, the in-chat card has a Send to landlord button, so the renter's own click is the yes. The honest limit is that the tool stays visible to the model, so a text-only host relies on the model obeying my words. Nothing inside send_to_landlord checks for a yes, so the gate is a rule I ask for, not a lock.
children.why: Sending tells a real landlord by email, and nobody can unsend that. The card button makes consent a click the renter did, which is stronger than trusting the model. Where no card appears, only the instructions stand in the way, and I say so plainly.

children.name: Idempotent send
children.one_liner: Sending twice changes nothing: the second call returns the status
children.explain: I check the contact first, and the rule depends on the channel the renter picked. Email must look like name@host.tld, sms needs at least 10 digits, and app needs a non-empty username or email. If the question is already waiting or replied, I return that status and send nothing, so a repeated call never sends twice. Otherwise I set the status to waiting, email the landlord, and send the renter a confirmation on their channel. For chat_only nothing goes to the renter, because that channel means they will check back in the chat.
children.why: A model can call a tool twice, and both the card and the model may try to send the same question. Returning the stored status turns a repeat into a harmless no-op, so the landlord gets one email per question. The tool is also annotated idempotent, meaning repeating it has no extra effect.

children.name: Reply becomes answer
children.one_liner: A landlord reply can be saved so later renters get it instantly
children.explain: When the landlord replies, landlord_reply checks the question is waiting for that landlord, then stores the reply and sets the status to replied. The landlord can also save the reply as a saved answer, for this unit only or for all their units, marked with source from_reply. Then I notify the renter on the channel they chose, and they can also read it in chat with check_landlord_reply. The next renter's ask_landlord reads every saved answer for that landlord, so the saved reply matches instantly with no wait.
children.why: Many renters ask a landlord the same things, so one slow reply can answer them all. Saving it turns that reply into an instant answer, and the landlord's queue shrinks over time. Without the save, each renter would wait for the same reply again.
